quote_orig: אֶפְרַ֙יִם֙ וּמְנַשֶּׁ֔ה כִּרְאוּבֵ֥ן וְשִׁמְע֖וֹן יִֽהְיוּ־לִֽי׃ וּמוֹלַדְתְּךָ֛ אֲשֶׁר־הוֹלַ֥דְתָּ אַחֲרֵיהֶ֖ם לְךָ֣ יִהְי֑וּ עַ֣ל שֵׁ֧ם אֲחֵיהֶ֛ם יִקָּרְא֖וּ בְּנַחֲלָתָֽם׃
quote_en: And now thy two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, which were born unto thee in the land of Egypt before I came unto thee into Egypt, are mine; as Reuben and Simeon, they shall be mine. 48:6 And thy issue, which thou begettest after them, shall be thine, and shall be called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance.
licence_note: Hebrew: Sefaria version 'Miqra according to the Masorah', license 'CC-BY-SA'. English: KJV, public domain; Gutenberg eBook #10 text.
keys: are mine; as Reuben and Simeon, they shall be mine
shall be called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance
what_it_shows: Jacob tells Joseph that his two sons born in Egypt, Ephraim and Manasseh, "shall be mine" as Reuben and Simeon are his, so the text counts them among Jacob's own sons. Children Joseph has later "shall be thine", but are "called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance".
context: Jacob, dying in Egypt, blesses Joseph and his sons (Gen 48:1-2). The two verses are one continuous speech; the first is the adoption-like declaration and the second limits what follows for later children.
limits: The verses use no word for adoption; the legal character is read into 'as Reuben and Simeon'. The two boys are Joseph's sons by birth in the same verse ('your two sons, who were born to you'), and the speaker is their grandfather, not an unrelated adoptive father. Verse 6 gives Joseph's later children a different rule: they are Joseph's by birth and are reckoned 'under the name' of Ephraim and Manasseh 'in their inheritance', so the text states a transfer by name for inheritance and does not say the later children become sons of Jacob. Hebrew 'על שם אחיהם' is 'upon the name of their brothers'; the KJV reads 'after the name'.
from_: And now thy two sons, Ephraim
to: of their brethren in their inheritance.

ref: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 3.12.4 (Whiston, Book III ch. 12 §4)
quote_en: Instead of Levi, Moses took Manasseh, the son of Joseph, among the heads of tribes; and Ephraim instead of Joseph. It was indeed the desire of Jacob himself to Joseph, that he would give him his sons to be his own by adoption, as I have before related.
licence_note: Whiston translation (1737), Project Gutenberg eBook #2848. Greek not read.
keys: to be his own by adoption
the son of Joseph
Ephraim instead of Joseph
what_it_shows: Josephus says that Jacob wished Joseph to give him his sons "to be his own by adoption", and in the census of Numbers 1 he says Ephraim was taken "instead of Joseph" and Manasseh "among the heads of tribes".
context: Josephus is retelling the census of Numbers 1, in which Moses counts the fighting men of the tribes, and the sentence is an aside back to the earlier account in Genesis 48 that he says he has already given.
limits: The same sentence calls Manasseh "the son of Joseph", and Joseph remains the father in the text; the source describes the arrangement as Jacob's desire and as an earlier event, not as a general rule. Whiston's note 15 on Antiquities 2.8.1 says that all copies of Genesis omit the encomium on Joseph that Josephus gives there and that Whiston did not know where Josephus took it "or whether it be not his own embellishment only" (this note concerns the encomium, not the adoption word). Greek not checked, so the translator's choice of the word "adoption" is unverified.
from_: Instead of Levi, Moses took Manasseh,
to: adoption, as I have before related.

quote_en: There is, however, one passage in Scripture (Gen. xlviii. 5), "Ephraim and Manasseh . . . are mine; as Reuben and Simeon, they shall be mine," which indicates that the writer was probably acquainted with Adoption in the legal sense, such as would give to the chosen children the right of inheriting from the person adopting them; for the obvious intent of the passage is to account for the establishment of two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, with distinct territories, on an equality with the tribes claiming descent from Jacob's sons.
licence_note: Public-domain 1901–1906 article text (Dembitz section signed L. N. D.); the website footer reads '©2002-2021 ... All rights reserved' (see work licence).
keys: indicates that the writer was probably acquainted with Adoption in the legal sense
to account for the establishment of two tribes
what_it_shows: The encyclopedia authors say that Gen 48:5 "indicates that the writer was probably acquainted with Adoption in the legal sense", because the passage accounts for Ephraim and Manasseh having tribal territories on an equality with the other tribes.
context: Section "Adoption in Female Line" of the article (Dembitz); the article first treats Talmudic rearing-parenthood, then Biblical examples.
limits: Commentator opinion, not the verse itself: the article says "probably" and treats the verse as indirect evidence. Against the thesis, the same article says: "The adrogatio of the older Roman law ... is unknown to both Biblical and Talmudic law" (verbatim, A5 read); and that the Levirate "shows that Adoption in the Roman sense did not exist among the ancient Hebrews" (verbatim: "In fact, the Mosaic institution of the Levirate , by which the surviving brother is enjoined to marry his deceased brother's wife in order to give him a male heir, shows that Adoption in the Roman sense did not exist among the ancient Hebrews"). It also says of Esther: "neither does it appear that a method for creating such a relation between them as would make her his heiress was ever known to the laws of Israel."
from_: There is, however, one passage in
to: tribes claiming descent from Jacob's sons.

quote_orig: לי הם. בְּחֶשְׁבּוֹן שְׁאָר בָּנַי הֵם, לִטֹּל חֵלֶק בָּאָרֶץ אִישׁ כְּנֶגְדּוֹ
own_translation_en: They are mine: in reckoning they count as my other sons, to take a share in the land, each one corresponding to his brother. (team translation of Rashi, Hebrew read)
licence_note: Sefaria version 'Pentateuch with Rashi's commentary by M. Rosenbaum and A.M. Silbermann, 1929-1934', license 'Public Domain'. No PD English read, so the English is the team's translation.
keys: בְּחֶשְׁבּוֹן שְׁאָר בָּנַי הֵם

what_it_shows: Rashi glosses 'they shall be mine' as meaning that Ephraim and Manasseh, 'in reckoning', are among Jacob's other sons so as to take a share of the land, each corresponding to one of his brothers.
context: Medieval commentary on the verse in A5-P02. It explains the verse, it is not Scripture, and it links the adoption to land division.
limits: Rashi's word 'in reckoning' (בְּחֶשְׁבּוֹן) describes counting for the purpose of land; the gloss says nothing about priesthood, royal status or the lineage of later descendants. Rashi is a commentator, not a legal source. Rashi on 48:6 not read.

quote_orig: וְלֹא־הָיָ֧ה לְשֵׁשָׁ֛ן בָּנִ֖ים כִּ֣י אִם־בָּנ֑וֹת וּלְשֵׁשָׁ֛ן עֶ֥בֶד מִצְרִ֖י וּשְׁמ֥וֹ יַרְחָֽע׃ וַיִּתֵּ֨ן שֵׁשָׁ֧ן אֶת־בִּתּ֛וֹ לְיַרְחָ֥ע עַבְדּ֖וֹ לְאִשָּׁ֑ה וַתֵּ֥לֶד ל֖וֹ אֶת־עַתָּֽי׃
quote_en: Now Sheshan had no sons, but daughters. And Sheshan had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Jarha. 2:35 And Sheshan gave his daughter to Jarha his servant to wife; and she bare him Attai.
licence_note: Hebrew: Sefaria version 'Miqra according to the Masorah', license 'CC-BY-SA'. English: KJV, public domain; Gutenberg eBook #10 text.
keys: Sheshan had no sons, but daughters
she bare him Attai
what_it_shows: The genealogy says Sheshan had only daughters and an Egyptian servant, Jarha; Sheshan gave his daughter to Jarha "to wife", and she bore him Attai, and the list then continues Attai's line in the Jerahmeel genealogy.
context: Chronicles gives a genealogy headed by "the sons of Jerahmeel" (2:33); the Sheshan episode sits inside that list.
limits: The text says nothing about adoption, legal sonship or the servant's son being counted as Sheshan's; it says only "she bare him Attai". The Jewish Encyclopedia reads this as adoption (its words: "adopted their sons as his own"), but that is the encyclopedia's gloss, not the verse. The line runs through a daughter's marriage to a non-Israelite servant, so this is a family arrangement with no stated legal act. The verses do not state a tribe for Attai in the text read.
from_: Now Sheshan had no sons, but
to: wife; and she bare him Attai.

ref: Sanhedrin 19b (Wikisource Talmud Bavli, R. Joshua b. Korha segment)
quote_orig: ור' יהושע בן קרחה נמי הכתיב את חמשת בני מיכל בת שאול אמר לך רבי יהושע וכי מיכל ילדה והלא מירב ילדה מירב ילדה ומיכל גידלה לפיכך נקראו על שמה ללמדך שכל המגדל יתום בתוך ביתו מעלה עליו הכתוב כאילו ילדו:
own_translation_en: R. Joshua b. Korha: 'Did Michal bear them? Did not Merab bear them? Merab bore them and Michal reared them; therefore they were called after her; this teaches that whoever rears an orphan in his house, Scripture counts it as if he had begotten him.' (team translation of the Hebrew)
licence_note: Wikisource Talmud Bavli (CC-BY-SA) Hebrew. Sefaria English not used (CC-BY-NC).
keys: שכל המגדל יתום בתוך ביתו
כאילו ילדו
what_it_shows: A rabbinic principle that the one who raises a child is counted as its parent, and the child is named after the rearer. The same page applies it to Ruth and Naomi, and, via Ps 77:16 (R. Eleazar), to Ephraim and Manasseh: "Jacob begat, and Joseph nourished, therefore they were called after his name" (team translation).
context: Sanhedrin 19b discusses David's marriages to Michal and Merab, then gives the Michal, Naomi and Ps 77:16 examples.
limits: Talmudic exegesis of biblical verses, not statute. The page records a dispute (R. Yosei reads the Michal verse differently) and the principle concerns honour and naming, not tribe, priesthood or royal rank. The Michal case is itself a dispute over who bore the children.
from_: ור' יהושע בן קרחה נמי הכתיב
to: ביתו מעלה עליו הכתוב כאילו ילדו:

ref: On the Life of Moses 1.19 (Yonge, CCEL section 19)
quote_en: And when the king's daughter saw that he was more perfect than could have been expected at his age, and when from his appearance she conceived greater good will than ever towards him, she adopted him as her son, having first put in practice all sorts of contrivances to increase the apparent bulk of her belly, so that he might be looked upon as her own genuine child, and not as a supposititious one; but God easily brings to pass whatever he is inclined to effect, however difficult it may be to bring to a successful issue.
licence_note: Yonge translation (1854–1890), CCEL page read; no licence line on that page.
keys: she adopted him as her son
so that he might be looked upon as her own genuine child
not as a supposititious one
what_it_shows: Philo says the king's daughter adopted Moses 'as her son', and that she first arranged a pretended pregnancy so that he would be 'looked upon as her own genuine child, and not as a supposititious one'.
context: A narrative of an Egyptian princess's decision in the story of Moses's infancy; Philo is retelling the Exodus infancy narrative for a Hellenistic reader (Exodus 2 itself not re-read in this session).
limits: The adoption is presented as a private act to make the child seem genuine; the text does not describe a legal rule of lineage. The same book makes Moses prefer his natural kin: see A5-P09 (Philo, Life of Moses 1.32–33): Philo calls the things 'thought good among those who had adopted him as spurious' and says Moses judged 'both of his real parents and of those who had adopted him'.
from_: And when the king's daughter saw
to: to bring to a successful issue.

quote_en: For our forefathers did not only appoint the best of these priests, and those that attended upon the Divine worship, for that design from the beginning, but made provision that the stock of the priests should continue unmixed and pure; for he who is partaker of the priesthood must propagate of a wife of the same nation, without having any regard to money, or any other dignities; but he is to make a scrutiny, and take his wife's genealogy from the ancient tables, and procure many witnesses to it.
licence_note: Whiston translation (1737), Project Gutenberg eBook #2849. Greek not read.
keys: the stock of the priests should continue unmixed and pure
take his wife's genealogy from the ancient tables
what_it_shows: Josephus says the priestly line was kept "unmixed and pure": a priest must marry a wife of the same nation, her genealogy is checked "from the ancient tables", and the priests send "the ancient names of their parents" to Jerusalem.
context: Josephus is describing Jewish record-keeping of priestly families (Jerusalem, Egypt, Babylon), to argue that Jewish histories are accurately recorded.
limits: The passage describes priestly purity by parents and ancestors and says nothing about adoption; this is argument from silence, not a denial. It concerns priestly status, not tribe, inheritance or royal lineage, and it shows the registers were kept by parentage, which bears against the claim that adoption transmits priesthood. The brief's location (Against Apion 1.30-36) is wrong for this passage.
from_: For our forefathers did not only
to: and procure many witnesses to it.

ref: On the Life of Moses 1.32–33 (Yonge, CCEL section 32–33)
quote_en: But Moses, having now reached the very highest point of human good fortune, and being looked upon as the grandson of this mighty king, and being almost considered in the expectations of all men as the future inheritor of his grandfather's kingdom, and being always addressed as the young prince, still felt a desire for and admiration of the education of his kinsmen and ancestors, considering all the things which were thought good among those who had adopted him as spurious, even though they might, in consequence of the present state of affairs, have a brilliant appearance; and those things which were thought good by his natural parents, even though they might be for a short time somewhat obscure, at all events akin to himself and genuine good things. (33) Accordingly, like an uncorrupt judge both of his real parents and of those who had adopted him,
licence_note: Yonge translation (1854–1890), CCEL page read; no licence line on that page.
keys: as the future inheritor of his grandfather's kingdom
those who had adopted him as spurious
what_it_shows: Philo says Moses was treated as 'the future inheritor of his grandfather's kingdom' while being raised by the king's daughter, but that he judged the adoptive education 'spurious' and cherished 'his real parents' as well as 'those who had adopted him'.
context: Continues the adoption narrative of 1.19; Philo presents Moses as choosing kinship by birth over the adoptive royal life.
limits: The text itself shows the adopted child's inheritance claim (the kingdom) was only a prospect, and that Moses rejects the adoptive identity. It does not say the adoptive status would have transferred his people's identity or tribe. Greek not checked.

to: of those who had adopted him,

ref: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 2.8.1 (Whiston, Book II ch. 8 §1)
quote_en: He then commanded his own sons that they should admit Joseph's sons, Ephraim and Manasses, into their number, and divide the land of Canaan in common with them
licence_note: Whiston translation (1737), Project Gutenberg eBook #2848. Greek not read.
keys: admit Joseph's sons, Ephraim and Manasses, into their number
divide the land of Canaan in common with them
what_it_shows: Josephus says Jacob told his own sons to "admit Joseph's sons, Ephraim and Manasses, into their number, and divide the land of Canaan in common with them", i.e. the two boys share in the land with Jacob's other sons.
context: Josephus is summarising Jacob's death in Book II, and this sentence reports the Genesis 48 arrangement in his own words; the same chapter says the sons are to be treated "hereafter" in his later account.
limits: Josephus's paraphrase, not the Genesis text: his sentence has no word for adoption, and Whiston's note 15 (on the encomium just before this sentence) says Genesis omits the encomium and Whiston does not know where Josephus took it. The source says the land is divided 'in common', which is an inheritance claim, and says nothing on priesthood or royal rank.
from_: He then commanded his own sons
to: of Canaan in common with them

ref: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 2.9.7 (Whiston, Book II ch. 9 §7); brief numbering 2.232-236
quote_en: Thermuthis therefore perceiving him to be so remarkable a child, adopted him for her son, having no child of her own. And when one time had carried Moses to her father, she showed him to him, and said she thought to make him her successor, if it should please God she should have no legitimate child of her own; and to him, "I have brought up a child who is of a divine form, 21 and of a generous mind; and as I have received him from the bounty of the river, in, I thought proper to adopt him my son, and the heir of thy kingdom.
licence_note: Whiston translation (1737), Project Gutenberg eBook #2848. Greek not read.
keys: adopted him for her son
the heir of thy kingdom
what_it_shows: In Josephus's Egyptian narrative the princess Thermuthis adopts the infant Moses "for her son" and says she will adopt him "my son, and the heir of thy kingdom".
context: A narrative set in the Egyptian court, not a statement of Israelite law: the adoption is the princess's decision, made because she has no child of her own. Moses is then presented as the foundling of the Hebrews.
limits: In the same narrative Moses refuses the diadem: Whiston has Josephus write that when the king placed it on his head, 'Moses threw it down to the ground', so the heir-of-kingdom claim does not take effect in the story. The adoption is by a non-Israelite, and the story says nothing about tribe or priestly status. Greek not checked. A stray number '21' appears in the middle of the quotation in the Gutenberg text; it is not checked against print.
from_: Thermuthis therefore perceiving him to be
to: and the heir of thy kingdom.

quote_en: The family from which I am derived is not an ignoble one, but hath descended all along from the priests; and as nobility among several people is of a different origin, so with us to be of the sacerdotal dignity, is an indication of the splendor of a family. Now, I am not only sprung from a sacerdotal family in general, but from the first of the twenty-four [1] courses; and as among us there is not only a considerable difference between one family of each course and another, I am of the chief family of that first course also; nay, further, by my mother I am of the royal blood; for the children of Asamoneus, from whom that family was derived, had both the office of the high priesthood, and the dignity of a king, for a long time together.
licence_note: Whiston translation (1737), Project Gutenberg eBook #2846; Gutenberg header 'This eBook is for the use of anyone anywhere...' read in the file.
keys: descended all along from the priests
by my mother I am of the royal blood
what_it_shows: Josephus traces his descent from priests through his fathers, says his mother was of royal blood through the Hasmonean house, and says he set out the genealogy 'as I have found it described in the public records'.
context: Josephus's own autobiographical claim of descent, written c. 99–100 CE, supported by public records; he gives the chain of fathers in detail.
limits: The lineage is by birth and by fathers' names; no adoption is mentioned, so the text is silent on whether adoption would count. The royal descent is said to come 'by my mother', which is a blood claim through the mother, not an adoption claim. The passage shows that public genealogies were kept by birth, which bears against an adoptive route to priesthood (see A5 Ag. Ap. 1.7).
from_: The family from which I am
to: king, for a long time together.

quote_en: And there were born to Joseph in Egypt before his father came into Egypt, those whom Asenath, daughter of Potiphar priest of Heliopolis bare unto him, Manasseh, and Ephraim—three.
licence_note: Charles 1913 (Oxford), OCR text read; licence not read on the page; public domain per the brief list. OCR shows '2s' for verse 25; the number is corrected here.
keys: those whom Asenath, daughter of Potiphar priest of Heliopolis bare unto him
born to Joseph in Egypt
what_it_shows: Jubilees, a 2nd-century BCE retelling, lists Manasseh and Ephraim as children "born to Joseph in Egypt" to Asenath, and counts them in the seventy souls of the house of Jacob.
context: Jubilees, a 2nd-century BCE retelling, lists the sons of Jacob and his sons' families on the way to Egypt; within that list it says Manasseh and Ephraim were born to Joseph in Egypt to Asenath.
limits: Here Jubilees gives the two boys as Joseph's children by birth; the passage does not mention Jacob adopting them. Searches of the Jubilees pages read (chapters 34 and 45 and the OCR) found no word for adoption. This is a LIMIT on any claim that Jubilees treats them as Jacob's adopted sons. Jubilees 45 says Joseph gave Jacob the right of dwelling in Goshen and in the region around Rameses, and says nothing about tribes.
from_: And there were born to Joseph
to: bare unto him, Manasseh, and Ephraim—three.

quote_en: our legislator admits all those that have a mind to observe our laws so to do; and this after a friendly manner, as esteeming that a true union which not only extends to our own stock, but to those that would live after the same manner with us; yet does he not allow those that come to us by accident only to be admitted into communion with us.
licence_note: Whiston translation (1737), Project Gutenberg eBook #2849. Greek not read.
keys: admits all those that have a mind to observe our laws
admitted into communion with us
what_it_shows: Josephus says the lawgiver "admits all those that have a mind to observe our laws" into the community, and does not admit those who come to them only "by accident".
context: Josephus is describing how Jewish law treats foreigners, in the middle of his defence of the Jewish laws.
limits: Admission is by adherence to the laws, not by lineage, tribe, inheritance or adoption; the passage names no tribe and no inheritance right. Read with A5-P07, priests must marry within the nation.
from_: our legislator admits all those that
to: be admitted into communion with us.

ref: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 1.154 (Whiston, Book I ch. 7 §1; brief numbering 1.154)
quote_en: Now Abram, having no son of his own, adopted Lot, his brother Haran's son, and his wife Sarai's brother; and he left the land of Chaldea when he was seventy-five years old, and at the command of God went into Canaan, and therein he dwelt himself, and left it to his posterity.
licence_note: Whiston translation (1737), Project Gutenberg eBook #2848. Greek not read; the 1.154 numbering is from the brief and was not checked.
keys: adopted Lot
having no son of his own
what_it_shows: Josephus says that Abram, "having no son of his own, adopted Lot, his brother Haran's son". The word "adopted" is Josephus's term for a nephew taken into the household.
context: Josephus introduces Abram and Lot and does not say that Lot was made an heir.
limits: Genesis 15:2-3 (KJV, read) has Abram say: "the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus? ... one born in my house is mine heir." Genesis gives the heir role to a house-born servant, not Lot, so Josephus's use of "adopted" is his own word and does not show inheritance by law. Hebrew of Gen 15 not read.

to: and left it to his posterity.
